title: Advanced Prototyping — Variables, Conditionals, Expressions
content:
Figma's advanced prototyping layer exists to solve one problem: representing STATE without duplicating frames.

THE THREE MECHANISMS:
- VARIABLES hold values that persist across frames. Four types: Boolean, Number, String, Color.
- CONDITIONALS evaluate an if/else boolean expression and branch which actions run.
- EXPRESSIONS compute values — arithmetic on numbers, concatenation on strings, comparison on booleans.

Plus two structural features they depend on:
- MULTIPLE ACTIONS — an unlimited stack of actions on one trigger, executed in listed order.
- INTERACTIVE COMPONENTS — variant switching in place via the Change to action.

WHAT THIS REPLACES: the frame explosion. A five-checkbox form goes from 32 frames and ~160 connections to one frame. A quantity stepper goes from ten frames to one. A multi-step form with validation goes from a branching tree to a handful of conditionals.

THE ORDERING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: on a single trigger, Set variable actions must come BEFORE the Conditional that reads them. Actions run top to bottom, so a conditional placed above the assignment evaluates the old value. This is the single most common bug in variable-driven Figma prototypes.

WHERE THE CEILING IS: no arrays, no loops, no functions, no persistence between sessions, no data fetching. Expressions do arithmetic, concatenation, and boolean logic. Past that, write code.

title: Variable Types and What Each Is For
content:
BOOLEAN — true/false. Bind to: layer visibility, component boolean properties, variant selection via conditionals. Use for: checkbox states, terms accepted, wallet connected, user logged in, feature flag, filter on/off, dark mode.

NUMBER — any number. Bind to: text content, width/height, spacing, corner radius, opacity, stroke weight, number component properties. Use for: cart quantity, item count, progress percentage, price, step index, volume level, token balance.

STRING — text. Bind to: text content, variant properties, component text properties. Use for: user name, selected option, entered email, current step label, selected size, wallet address, chosen network.

COLOR — a colour value with mode support. Bind to: fills, strokes, effects. Use for: theming, selection highlight, status colour (pending/confirmed/failed), brand switching.

BINDING: select the layer property → right-click or use the variable picker → choose the variable. A bound property shows the variable name instead of a raw value. Bound text content updates live in the prototype the moment the variable changes.

SCOPING AND HYGIENE:
- Keep prototype-only variables in a separate collection ('Prototype State') from your design tokens ('Primitives', 'Semantic'). Mixing them pollutes the token export and confuses engineering about what is a design decision versus a prototype mechanic.
- Name them like code: camelCase, descriptive, typed by prefix where useful — isWalletConnected, cartQuantity, selectedVariant, userEmail.
- Set a sensible default value. The default is what the prototype starts with on every playthrough, and it is how you define your empty state.

title: The Set Variable Action
content:
Set variable assigns a new value to a variable when a trigger fires. The 'to:' field accepts either a literal or an EXPRESSION.

PATTERNS:
- TOGGLE a boolean: set isOpen to `not isOpen`. One interaction handles both open and close.
- INCREMENT a number: set cartQuantity to `cartQuantity + 1`. Decrement with `- 1`.
- CLAMP an increment: pair it with a conditional — if `cartQuantity < maxStock` then set cartQuantity to `cartQuantity + 1`. Without the clamp your stepper counts to infinity, which is a real bug you will otherwise ship.
- ASSIGN a selection: set selectedSize to `"M"`. String literals need quotation marks.
- COMPUTE a derived value: set subtotal to `unitPrice * cartQuantity`. Set total to `subtotal + shipping`.
- BUILD a string: set greeting to `"Welcome back, " + userName`. Numbers can be appended to strings directly.
- RESET: a Set variable action returning a variable to its default is how you build 'Clear filters', 'Start over', and 'Log out'.

CAPTURING TEXT INPUT: bind a variable to a text layer's content inside a frame set as a text input, and the variable receives what the user types. This is the only way to make typing work in a Figma prototype, and it is what makes form-validation prototypes possible.

MULTIPLE SETS ON ONE TRIGGER: entirely normal and often necessary. 'Add to cart' typically sets cartQuantity, sets subtotal, sets lastAddedItem, then opens the cart drawer — four actions, one trigger, in that order.

title: Expression Syntax — Complete Reference
content:
Expressions are available in the Set variable 'to:' field and the Conditional 'if:' field. Invalid expressions are outlined in red.

NUMERIC — operands: number variables and number literals (0.5, 1, 10). Operators: `+` `-` `*` `/`. Negative numbers use a `-` prefix. Example: `subTotal * salesTax`.

STRING — operands: string literals in quotes, number literals, string and number variables. Operator: `+` for concatenation. Example: `"Welcome back " + userName`.

BOOLEAN — operands: `true` / `false`, number literals, string literals, and Boolean/String/Number variables. Operators:
- `==` equal to
- `!=` not equal to
- `>` greater than
- `<` less than
- `>=` greater than or equal to
- `<=` less than or equal to
- `and` logical AND
- `or` logical OR
- `!` or `not` negation
Example: `itemCount > 5 and isAvailable == true`.

ORDER OF OPERATIONS
Mathematical: parentheses → multiplication/division → addition/subtraction, left to right.
Boolean: parentheses → comparisons → AND → OR, left to right.
Use parentheses liberally; `a or b and c` does not mean what most people read it as.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST: arrays, objects, loops, functions, string methods (no length, no contains, no substring), date maths, random, modulo, rounding. If you need any of these, either restructure the problem into booleans or leave Figma.

title: Conditionals — If/Else Branching in Prototypes
content:
A conditional is an action that checks a boolean expression and runs nested actions only if it evaluates true. Add an Else branch for the false case, and chain Else-if branches for multiple outcomes.

STRUCTURE:
```
On click:
  Set variable  attempts = attempts + 1
  Conditional
    if  email != "" and password != ""
      → Navigate to  Dashboard
    else if  email == ""
      → Set variable  errorMessage = "Enter your email"
      → Navigate to  Login (error state)
    else
      → Set variable  errorMessage = "Enter your password"
      → Navigate to  Login (error state)
```

RULES:
- The Set variable that the conditional reads must appear ABOVE the conditional. Actions run in order.
- The expression must resolve to true or false. A conditional on a number ('if cartQuantity') is invalid; write 'if cartQuantity > 0'.
- Conditionals can nest, but two levels is the practical readability limit. Deeper logic belongs in code.
- Each branch can contain any actions, including further Set variables, Navigate to, Open overlay, and Change to.

WHAT THIS BUYS YOU: form validation, gated CTAs, multi-select with a minimum, quantity limits, feature gating by login state, conditional routing based on user choices, error states that reflect the actual mistake rather than a generic message. All of it in one frame per screen instead of one frame per combination.

THE HIDDEN VALUE: your conditionals ARE the business logic. Written out, they become the acceptance criteria engineering needs. Copy them into the handoff verbatim.

title: Variable Modes in Prototypes — Theming and Locale Switching
content:
The Set variable mode action switches the variable mode of a page mid-prototype. Every layer bound to a variable in that collection updates instantly.

WHAT IT UNLOCKS:
- A REAL theme toggle. One button, one action, and the whole prototype flips light↔dark. No duplicated frames, no duplicated components.
- BRAND SWITCHING for multi-brand systems — the same layout rendered in each brand's tokens, which is the fastest way to prove a multi-brand token architecture actually works.
- LOCALE / LANGUAGE switching via string variable modes, which exposes text-expansion breakage (German is typically 30% longer than English) in a way no static mock does.
- DENSITY switching (compact / comfortable) if your spacing tokens have modes.
- A/B COMPARISON — two modes of the same semantic tokens, toggled live in a stakeholder review.

MECHANICS AND CAVEATS:
- Mode applies at the PAGE level in prototypes, so it affects everything on the page, not just the current frame.
- The mode persists as the prototype navigates, which is what you want for a theme.
- Nested collections resolve through their own mode settings; if your semantic collection has modes but your primitive collection does not, only the semantic layer switches.
- Combine with a Boolean variable (isDarkMode) if you also need conditional logic keyed on the theme.

THIS IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE FEATURE FOR DESIGN SYSTEM WORK IN FIGMA. A live theme toggle in a prototype is the single most persuasive demonstration that a token architecture is sound, and the fastest way to find the places it is not.

title: Interactive Components — Building Stateful Components
content:
An interactive component carries its own state transitions internally via the Change to action, so every instance behaves correctly with no per-instance wiring.

HOW TO BUILD ONE:
1. Create a component set with the variants you need (Default, Hover, Pressed, Focus, Disabled, or Unchecked/Checked).
2. Select a variant, go to the Prototype tab, drag a connection to another variant in the same set.
3. Set the trigger and choose Change to.
4. Repeat for each transition. A button typically needs: Default → Hover (Mouse enter), Hover → Default (Mouse leave), Hover → Pressed (Mouse down), Pressed → Hover (Mouse up).

STATE BEHAVIOUR — THE PART THAT BITES:
- STATE IS MEMORISED. An instance remembers its last variant when you navigate away and back. Correct for a nav tab, wrong for a form.
- STATE IS SHARED. After the first interaction, matching components across frames synchronise. Correct for a persistent toggle, wrong for two independent checkboxes that happen to be the same component.
- Fix both with 'RESET COMPONENT STATE' in the interaction details panel of the interaction that navigates into the frame.

NESTED INSTANCES: a Change to on a nested instance can switch the PARENT component's variant. This is how you make a row's chevron collapse the accordion that contains it.

INTERACTION PRIORITY: if a prototype interaction and a variant interaction share the same trigger, the prototype interaction wins. If they use different triggers, both fire.

MAINTENANCE: edit variant interactions on the MAIN component. Instance-level variant overrides are not reflected in Presentation view.
source: help.figma.com — Create interactive components with variants

title: Variables + Interactive Components — The Combination That Scales
content:
Interactive components handle LOCAL state (this button is hovered). Variables handle GLOBAL state (the user has accepted terms). Combining them is what makes a Figma prototype feel like software.

THE CANONICAL PATTERN — a gated CTA:
1. Boolean variable `hasAcceptedTerms`, default false.
2. Checkbox is an interactive component with Unchecked/Checked variants, wired with Change to on click.
3. On the same click, add a second action: Set variable `hasAcceptedTerms` to `not hasAcceptedTerms`.
4. The submit Button component has a boolean component property for disabled state, bound to `hasAcceptedTerms`.
Result: checking the box enables the button, with no conditionals and no extra frames. One checkbox, one button, one variable.

MORE OF THE SAME SHAPE:
- SELECTED COUNT: each selectable card is an interactive component; its click also sets `selectedCount = selectedCount + 1` on select and `- 1` on deselect. A text layer bound to `selectedCount` updates live, and a conditional gates 'Continue' on `selectedCount > 0`.
- VARIANT PICKER (Shopify): swatches are an interactive component; clicking sets `selectedColor`. Bind `selectedColor` to the product image's variant property and to the price text. One frame, every combination.
- WALLET STATE (crypto): `isWalletConnected` boolean drives the header component's variant, the CTA's label, and the visibility of the balance block — every surface updates from one action.

THE PRINCIPLE: bind the variable to a COMPONENT PROPERTY rather than writing conditionals wherever possible. Property binding is declarative and maintains itself; conditionals are imperative and multiply.

title: Prototyping Real Text Input
content:
By default, typing in a Figma prototype does nothing. To make input work:

1. Create a String variable for the field (e.g. `emailInput`), default `""`.
2. Bind the input's text layer content to that variable.
3. Make the frame a text input in the Prototype tab so it accepts keyboard entry.
4. The variable now holds whatever the participant types, and any layer bound to it updates.

WHAT THIS ENABLES:
- Genuine validation. `if emailInput == ""` → empty error; `if emailInput != "" and hasAtSign == false` → format error (you will need a separate boolean, since expressions have no string methods).
- Personalisation across screens. `"Hi " + firstName` on the confirmation page, using what they actually typed.
- Search behaviour. Set a boolean when the field is non-empty and use a conditional to switch between the empty-search and results states.
- Character-limit feedback, by pairing with a number variable you increment per interaction (crude, but enough to demo the pattern).

LIMITS TO PLAN AROUND:
- No string length, no contains, no regex. Real format validation cannot be expressed. Prototype the STATES (valid, invalid, empty) and drive them with booleans set by explicit choices, then specify the actual validation rules in handoff.
- No masking or formatting. A card-number field will not chunk into groups of four; a wallet address will not truncate.
- No autofill, no browser validation, no keyboard type switching.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS: in usability testing, a form the participant can actually type into removes the biggest source of prototype-induced confusion. Build variable-backed input for the two or three fields the study depends on and pre-fill the rest.

title: Modelling State Before You Build
content:
Wiring variables without designing the state model first produces prototypes nobody can maintain. Ten minutes of modelling saves hours.

THE METHOD:
1. LIST THE STATES the screen can be in. Not the screens — the states. A product page: no variant selected, variant selected in stock, variant selected out of stock, added to cart, quantity at max.
2. IDENTIFY WHAT DISTINGUISHES THEM. Each distinguishing fact becomes one variable. Above: `selectedVariant` (string), `isInStock` (boolean), `cartQuantity` (number).
3. WRITE THE TRANSITIONS. From which state, on what trigger, to which state, setting which variables. This is a state table and it is exactly what an engineer wants.
4. DEFINE ILLEGAL STATES and how you prevent them. `cartQuantity > stockLevel` must be impossible — that is a clamp conditional, not a hope.
5. DEFINE THE INITIAL STATE. Variable defaults. This is your empty state and it deserves as much design attention as the ideal state.

WHY THIS IS DESIGN WORK, NOT ENGINEERING WORK: the illegal states and the initial state are where products actually break, and they are invisible in a static mock. A designer who arrives with a state table has pre-answered the questions engineering would otherwise resolve by guessing.

MINIMUM VARIABLE PRINCIPLE: use the fewest variables that distinguish the states. Two booleans express four states. Three express eight. If you have six booleans for five states, some are derivable and should be conditionals instead.

title: Advanced Prototype Recipes — Variables and Conditionals
content:
CLICK COUNTER WITH A THRESHOLD. Number variable `clicks` = 0. On click: Set `clicks` to `clicks + 1`; then Conditional `if clicks >= 5` → Navigate to success. Bind `clicks` to a text layer for live feedback.

QUANTITY STEPPER WITH LIMITS. Plus button: Conditional `if qty < maxStock` → Set `qty` to `qty + 1`. Minus: Conditional `if qty > 1` → Set `qty` to `qty - 1`. Bind `qty` to text; bind a derived `lineTotal = unitPrice * qty` to the price.

MULTI-SELECT WITH MINIMUM. Each option is an interactive component (Change to) plus Set variable `selected = selected ± 1`. Continue button: Conditional `if selected > 0` → Navigate to next; else → Open overlay error.

FORM VALIDATION WITH SPECIFIC ERRORS. String variables per field. On submit: Conditional chain — `if field1 == "none" or field2 == "none"` → error frame; else → success. Set a String `errorMessage` in each branch and bind it to the error text so the message is specific.

VOLUME / RANGE CONTROL WITHOUT FRAMES. Number variable `level`. Bind it to a rectangle's WIDTH. Plus/minus set `level + 5` / `level - 5`, clamped with conditionals at 0 and 100.

THEME TOGGLE. Boolean `isDark` plus Set variable mode. On click: Set `isDark` to `not isDark`; Set variable mode → Dark (or Light) — the boolean is only needed if other logic reads the theme.

CART DRAWER. Number `cartCount`, Number `cartSubtotal`. Add to cart: Set `cartCount + 1`; Set `cartSubtotal + price`; Open overlay cart. Badge and totals bind to the variables, so every surface stays consistent.

WALLET CONNECT. Boolean `isConnected`, String `address`, Number `balance`. Connect: Set all three; header component's variant property binds to `isConnected`, so the whole app updates from one interaction.

title: Where Variables and Conditionals Run Out
content:
KNOW THE CEILING so you stop before you waste a day.

NOT AVAILABLE:
- Arrays or lists. You cannot model 'the items in the cart'. You can model a count and a subtotal; you cannot model an arbitrary set of line items with individual quantities. Three hard-coded line-item components with individual variables is the practical workaround.
- Loops or iteration. No repeating over items.
- String methods. No length, contains, substring, uppercase, split. Real email or address validation is impossible.
- Maths beyond the four operators. No rounding, modulo, min/max, random, or percentage helpers. Rounding a currency value to two decimals cannot be done.
- Date and time. No now(), no arithmetic on dates.
- Persistence. Variables reset to defaults on every fresh playthrough. Nothing survives a reload.
- Network or data. No fetch, no API, no live prices, no real inventory.
- Reading a variable's value out to a viewer other than via a bound layer.

SYMPTOMS YOU HAVE HIT THE CEILING:
- More than about a dozen prototype variables.
- Conditionals nested three deep.
- A separate boolean invented for every possible combination.
- Hard-coding three line items because you cannot express a list.
- Spending longer on the wiring than on the design.

THE MOVE: switch to a code prototype using your real component library. You will get real data, real validation, real performance, and a prototype an engineer can read. Keep Figma for the flow, the states inventory, and the visual spec.
